seed: Shannon Byrne Susko, System by System post Build Up Your 3-5 Differentiators and worksheet; training of 27-Sep-2026; Byron Darlison, How I Create Strategy; Activity Fit Map playbook, Byron’s rulings of 27-Sep, 30-Sep and 9-Oct-2026 (name, keep 3 to 5, then draw dependencies from the most connected; a group with no lines; descriptor; sleep on it), order confirmed by Byron, 25-Nov-2026.

slides.title: Build your Activity Fit Map in four steps.
slides.support: To create your white space, you must invest in some things and give up others. Those are your activities.

artwork.alt: Four small pictures in a row. 1, write the activities: loose notes, everything you must do to create your white space. 2, group them and name each group: the notes sit around five named circles. The name sums up what the group does. 3, keep 3 to 5 groups: four circles take a color and one is struck out. These are your differentiators. 4, draw the lines: lines join the differentiators. They depend on each other. They become your swim lanes.

notes: Start from the white space the team just agreed on. To create it, the company must invest in some things and give up others. Those are the activities.
Walk the four steps. The team brainstorms every activity, groups them and names each group. It keeps 3 to 5. Those are the differentiators. Then it draws the lines.
This is the Activity Fit Map. The idea is Michael Porter’s: strategy is the set of activities a company does differently from its competitors. Shannon Susko builds it from the ground up.
Do not start from the attributes at the top of the 3HAG line and work down. That gives generic names.
The lines are the point. Differentiators that depend on each other are hard to copy. With no lines, the team has a list of capabilities.
The end is a map of what the company must do to create its 3HAG. The 3 to 5 differentiators become the swim lanes: what must get done, quarter by quarter, over the next three years.
The next four slides take one step each. The last one shows a finished example.
slides.headline: Build your Activity Fit Map in four steps.

slides.title: What must you do to make the whole 3HAG line true?
slides.support: Each leader writes 5 to 7 activities alone, one on each sticky note.
body: A differentiator is a group of activities that makes your 3HAG line true.
The whole line: where you will lead, what you will maintain and what you will let drop.
An activity can be something to stop doing.
Present your activities. Put them all on the board.
notes: The objective is to build the company’s 3 to 5 differentiators from the ground up. Do not start from the attributes at the top of the line and work down. That gives generic answers.
Keep asking the one question: what activities need to be in place to make the whole 3HAG line true?
Each leader presents their activities. Start grouping similar ones as they go up.
slides.headline: What must you do to make the whole 3HAG line true?

artwork.alt: Step 1 of the example. Loose notes on a board, one activity on each, not yet grouped.

slides.title: Group the activities. Name each group.
slides.support: Most teams end up with 4 to 6 groups.
body: Name each group for exactly what it will accomplish.
“Support” is too generic. Ask again: what will this group accomplish?
notes: Name each group together. The name says what will be true when that group of activities is in place.
Ask why the group matters. Expect to ask about five times before the name tells the team’s own story.
Do not skip this step. Take the time it needs.
Do not ask the team to tell the strategy yet. That comes after the lines are drawn.
slides.headline: Group the activities. Name each group.

artwork.alt: Step 2 of the example. The same notes now sit around five named groups: A Named Person for 90 Days, Live in a Day, Standard, Not Custom, One Flat Price and New Billing System.

slides.title: Agree on your 3 to 5 differentiators.
slides.support: Keep the strongest groups. Each one heads a swim lane.
body: Check back against your 3HAG line: every place you will lead has a group behind it.
Each one serves a need of your Core Customer.
A group you do not keep can stay as a supporting activity.
Give each a short descriptor: what is true when you achieve it.
notes: Most teams end up with 4 to 6 groups. Agree on the 3 to 5 that carry the strategy before anyone draws an arrow.
Check each group back against the Attribution Framework. Which chosen attribute does it move? Which Core Customer need does it serve?
A group that connects to nothing the market values is a task, not a differentiator.
The descriptor heads the swim lane. It keeps the team aligned after people forget the workshop.
In the example, New Billing System is not kept. It is a task. It serves no place where the company will lead.
slides.headline: Agree on your 3 to 5 differentiators.

artwork.alt: Step 3 of the example. Four groups are kept and take a color: A Named Person for 90 Days, Live in a Day, Standard, Not Custom and One Flat Price. New Billing System fades and is marked not kept.

slides.title: Draw the lines: what depends on what?
slides.support: If you cannot do this one, can you still win with that one? If not, draw a line and write why. Then tell your strategy with the names and the lines.

artwork.alt: The finished example Activity Fit Map. Four colored circles sit around a dashed circle that reads: tell the strategy with the names and the lines. A Named Person for 90 Days has three activities: a single contact, a call in week one, answers in one day. Live in a Day has two: guided setup, ready-made templates. Standard, Not Custom has three: one product for all, no custom work, a short, fixed report set. One Flat Price has two: one plan, no add-ons. Three lines carry a reason. A Named Person for 90 Days to Live in a Day: a fast start leaves time for the customer. Live in a Day to Standard, Not Custom: one product makes setup fast. Standard, Not Custom to One Flat Price: no custom work keeps one price. Under the map, a key for reading the lines. All joined: one strategy, hard to copy. One left alone: it sets you apart, or it is a task. None joined: a list of capabilities.

notes: Draw the lines only between the 3 to 5 the team kept. A line joins two differentiators. It does not join two activities.

A line means one depends on the other. Start with the most-connected differentiator. For each of the others, ask: if we cannot do that one, can we win with this one? Draw the line when the team agrees.
A line has no arrow. Say which one depends on which. A differentiator can depend on more than one other.
Write the reason on the line. This is Darlison practice, not Shannon’s. It makes the team say why.
Then read the lines. They answer one question: is this one strategy, or a list?
All joined: the differentiators work as one set. A competitor who copies one piece gets little.
One left alone: it is either what sets the company apart or a task. Ask the team to tell you more. If it is still unclear, leave it where it is.
None joined: the team has a list of capabilities. It is rare to get this far and find that.
Last, one leader tells the company’s strategy aloud, using only the names and the lines. If the story does not hold, fix a name or a line.
Telling the strategy after the lines is Darlison practice. Shannon tests the names alone, before the lines.

When the lines are drawn, the team has a map of what it must do to create its 3HAG. The 3 to 5 differentiators become the swim lanes: what must get done, quarter by quarter, over the next three years.
In the example, Live in a Day and One Flat Price each depend on Standard, Not Custom. A Named Person for 90 Days depends on Live in a Day.
The example is the same subscription company as before. Its 3HAG line leads on speed of setup, price predictability and support from a person. Reporting and customization drop.
This is an example. Do not recommend these differentiators to a team.
Take a break here. After it, the team writes its new 3HAG. The differentiators go into it, in place of the key capabilities.
Let the team sleep on the differentiators before they are final. Day 2 opens by asking what anyone would change.
slides.headline: Draw the lines: what depends on what?
